questions.question: Oliver, you've called this novel 'brilliant entertainment' and I want to start there — because that feels almost like a provocation. When you read that line about Lucilla's 'calmest and most profound conviction' that her own plans are the most interesting thing in the room, are you genuinely saying the whole joke is just — she's deluded and it's funny? Because that seems almost too easy for a novel this good.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to commit fully to the comedy reading before Daniel can complicate it — sets up the central disagreement immediately

questions.question: Daniel, I can hear you itching to respond to that. Because your take is essentially the opposite — you're saying Lucilla isn't deluded at all. She's *right* about her own importance, and that's actually the darkest thing about the book. Can you unpack that? How does a novel being warm toward its heroine become, as you put it, 'the most damning thing about it'?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's class-ideology reading in direct contrast to Oliver's comedy reading — force the core disagreement into the open

questions.question: Edmund, you've been listening to both of them and I suspect you think they're both half-wrong. You called this a 'Johnsonian' portrait — which is a very specific claim. What does Johnson give you that 'comic genius' or 'class critique' doesn't, when you're reading that opening passage?
questions.intent: Give Edmund room to articulate his moral-character reading as a genuine third position, not just a tiebreaker — the Johnson comparison is rich and needs drawing out

questions.question: Let's get into the contralto passage — c4:p72 — because all three of you want to quote it and you all hear something different in it. Oliver, you said you have to *hear* it to feel it, that the prose is performing Lucilla's vanity. Would you read it for us and tell us what you're listening for?
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud, then immediately open it to competing interpretations — Daniel sees cold resource-auditing, Edmund sees genuine taste, Oliver sees comic mimicry

questions.question: One last thing I want to push on — that 'new luminary' line, c3:p18. Daniel, you said the irony is darker than it looks because the novel actually *vindicates* Lucilla in the end. But Oliver thinks Oliphant is winking at Victorian transformation rhetoric. Edmund thinks she's not really doing either. So who's right about what Oliphant knows she's doing — is this a writer in control of a dark joke, or a writer who genuinely loves her character too much to see it clearly?
questions.intent: Force all three to commit to a position on Oliphant's own awareness and intention — the authorial consciousness question cuts across all three readings and should produce genuine three-way friction

steering_notes: The productive tension in this segment is a three-way split that maps cleanly: Oliver wants comedy, Daniel wants ideology, Edmund wants moral psychology — and all three are using the same two or three passages as evidence. Keep returning the conversation to the text rather than the abstractions. The contralto passage is the best flashpoint because it's the one where the disagreement is most concrete: is Lucilla auditing human resources (Daniel), composing a symphony (Oliver), or demonstrating genuine taste (Edmund)? Let that question do the work. Watch for Oliver and Daniel to talk past each other — they're actually arguing about whether self-delusion and class consensus are the same thing, which is more interesting than either of them has quite said yet. Edmund is the wildcard who could either defuse or detonate depending on when you bring him in.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's claim that Lucilla 'isn't wrong about her importance within her social world' directly contradicts Oliver's reading of her as comically deluded — these two positions need to meet head-on early
Oliver's 'force of nature' framing vs Daniel's 'instrument of class reproduction' framing: same character, opposite metaphors — worth naming explicitly

Edmund's pushback on both colleagues — that they're each guilty of missing the 'particular soul' for the system — is itself a position Daniel will want to dispute, since Edmund's 'timeless human will' reading is exactly what Daniel thinks lets ideology off the hook
All three want to quote c2:p15 but with completely different tones of voice — getting them to read it or describe how it should be read could be a lively moment

segment_name: The Architecture of Society: Class and Influence in Miss Marjoribanks

questions.question: Daniel, you flagged the word 'commanding' in the description of Dr Marjoribanks's house — 'commanding as it did all Grange Lane' — and said that's not about hosting dinner parties, that's surveillance. But Oliver wants to read that same passage aloud with the gravity of Wellington at Waterloo, as pure comedy. Are those two readings actually compatible, or does the joke require us to look away from something real?
questions.intent: Force the first confrontation between Rosen's power-critique and Trevelyan's comic reading on a specific shared passage — establish the central tension of the segment early

questions.question: Oliver, you said you want to deliver 'Dr Marjoribanks's house could not have been better placed as a strategic position' with the gravity of Wellington discussing Waterloo — that the comedy comes from treating domestic management as military conquest. But here's what I want to push on: does the joke only land if we're already on Lucilla's side? Because if Daniel's right about what 'commanding' actually means, are we laughing *with* the narrator or are we being managed by her the same way Carlingford is?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to defend or complicate his complicity argument — that we're made to find Lucilla's absurdity delightful — and open the question of what the narrator is actually doing to the reader

questions.question: Edmund, you said 'almost Utopian' is Oliphant's irony — that little word 'almost' is where the author asks whether Lucilla's benevolence is sincere or merely instrumental. But Oliver says the irony is comic, Daniel says the benevolence is a con. You seem to be saying it's a genuinely moral question, not a joke and not an exposure. What does the novel actually think benevolence *is* — and is Lucilla's version of it good enough?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's moral-drama reading as a distinct third position, not just a middle ground — get him to make the positive case that this is a conscience novel, not a satire or a critique

questions.question: Edmund, you want to quote the 'sublime despondency' passage — Lucilla weeping alone after what looks like triumph — and you read it as Oliphant revealing the spiritual cost of ambition. Daniel reads those exact tears as 'the lubricant of exploitation,' pity that makes the system run smoother. Oliver thinks it's performative emotion, theatrical even to herself. So whose Lucilla is crying, and does it matter?
questions.intent: Put all three readings of c27:p57 into direct collision — this is the passage where the disagreements are sharpest and most productive, and naming all three positions simultaneously should produce genuine three-way debate

questions.question: Daniel, you said the ironic narrator who watches Lucilla's tears with 'knowing sympathy' is complicit — that we're meant to admire her intelligence while staying blind to what that intelligence does to the people below her. But that framing makes Oliphant sound like she's writing propaganda for soft power without realising it. Is that really what you think? Because that's a pretty extraordinary claim about a novelist who's clearly in on the joke — where does Oliphant's own intelligence sit in all this?
questions.intent: Push Rosen to the edge of his argument — is Oliphant radical or is she complicit, and can she be both? This should produce his strongest and most provocative take, and invite Trevelyan and Leigh to defend the author

steering_notes: The three positions map cleanly onto the same passages — especially 'almost Utopian,' 'commanding,' and the c27:p57 tears — so keep returning to the text rather than letting the conversation drift into abstraction. Trevelyan's performative readings are great radio; push him to actually *do* the voices when quoting. Rosen is the most provocative and should be challenged rather than allowed to lecture — the best moments will come when Leigh or Trevelyan force him to specify what Oliphant herself understood. Leigh is at risk of being the reasonable middle, so push him toward a strong positive claim about the moral drama rather than letting him just moderate. Don't let 'irony' become a weasel word — every time someone says it, ask them to show it in the sentence.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen says the narrator is complicit in Lucilla's soft power; Trevelyan says the narrator is ironic and comic — these are direct contradictions about the same narrative voice, not just different emphases

Leigh reads 'almost Utopian' as a genuine moral question about sincerity; Trevelyan reads it as the site of deadpan comedy; Rosen reads it as ideological cover — all three need to be in the room at once on that single phrase

Trevelyan argues we're made complicit in finding Lucilla's absurdity *delightful*; Rosen argues we're made blind to what her intelligence does to those below her — these are the same observation from opposite moral positions and the experts should be told that explicitly

The c27:p57 tears are cited by all three experts as their key evidence — this is the single best cross-engagement moment in the segment and should be saved for the fourth question when positions are already established

segment_name: Scandal and Structure: The Cavendish Affair Unravels

questions.question: Oliver, you've described the moment at c33:p25 — where Cavendish gets called a 'criminal' and a 'conspirator' and his genuine shock actually saves him — as the pivot of the whole scandal. Can you read that passage and explain what you mean? Because it seems almost farcical that the Archdeacon's *overreach* is what lets Cavendish off the hook.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c33:p25 aloud and make the case for comic structure — sets up immediate tension with Edmund's tragic reading and Daniel's systemic reading

questions.question: Edmund, you've used the word 'tragedy' about Cavendish — Aristotelian tragedy, no less. But Oliver's just suggested this is closer to farce, that Cavendish is basically a man who keeps tripping over his own feet. And there's that passage at c29:p45 — 'he could rather be content to lose them all at a stroke… than that Carlingford should find out that he was not, after all, one of the Cavendishes' — is that a tragic hero, or is that just a man with a particularly lethal form of vanity?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to defend the tragic reading against Oliver's comic one while getting the c29:p45 quote on the table — also primes Daniel's systemic challenge

questions.question: Daniel, you've said something genuinely provocative in our chat beforehand — that Cavendish's real crime isn't the lie, it's getting caught in a way that forces the system to *acknowledge* the lie publicly. You've got a line I want you to find — c32:p22, 'his favourite adventurer, the impostor whom he had denounced' — and you made a big deal of that word 'favourite.' What's going on there? Because it sounds like you're saying the Archdeacon knew all along.
questions.intent: Get Daniel to read c32:p22 and make the systemic argument explicit — the scandal exposes not Cavendish's corruption but the system's — directly challenges both Edmund's moral psychology and Oliver's pathology reading

questions.question: All three of you keep circling back to Lucilla and c28:p78 — 'the calmness of a knowledge which was aware of all and had nothing more to discover.' Oliver, you called her an oracle. Daniel thinks she's the system's perfect instrument. Edmund thinks she's a figure of genuine moral wisdom. Can you read that line and tell me honestly: is Lucilla *above* this mess, or is she the most deeply implicated person in the room?
questions.intent: Get c28:p78 read aloud and force a three-way confrontation about what Lucilla's calm actually means — the sharpest cross-engagement point between all three experts

questions.question: Last one — and I want to push on this. Edmund, you've argued that the Barbara Lake visit at c47:p28 isn't political miscalculation, it's the public inscription of an already-ruined interior. But Oliver thinks it's just a man who can't stop himself, and Daniel thinks it's a system making an example of someone. Which is it — soul, stupidity, or structure?
questions.intent: Force a three-way showdown on the Lake house scene with a deliberately reductive either/or framing — designed to produce all three experts talking over each other and a genuinely energetic close to the segment

steering_notes: The big energy in this segment comes from the comedy-versus-tragedy fault line between Oliver and Edmund — keep returning to it because it's the most viscerally disagreeable point and both are committed to their reading. Daniel's systemic argument is the wild card that destabilises both: let him interrupt whenever Edmund or Oliver sound like they're settling. The three c28:p78, c29:p45, and c33:p25 passages are all wanted by multiple experts — when one reads a passage, invite another to respond to the same lines immediately. Don't let any single expert have a passage to themselves. Watch for the moment Daniel accuses Edmund of aestheticising a structural problem — that's the flashpoint.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund calls Cavendish's preference for ruin over exposure a 'spiritual' matter — Daniel will want to call this mystification of a class mechanism, push them to argue this directly after Edmund quotes c29:p45

Oliver says Cavendish's 'amazement' at c33:p25 isn't deep character work but a miscalculation — Edmund thinks it's a man whose soul has already betrayed him. They are describing the same moment in mutually exclusive terms. Make them name the disagreement explicitly.

Daniel's 'favourite adventurer' reading at c32:p22 implies the Archdeacon was complicit — Oliver's reading of the same scene emphasises the Archdeacon's overreach as comic miscalculation. These two need to argue about whether the Archdeacon is a hypocrite or a fool, or both.

All three experts want Lucilla's c28:p78 passage but mean completely different things by it — use this as the segment's centrepiece moment, read it once, then let each expert respond in turn without interruption

segment_name: Wit as Weapon: Oliphant's Comic Voice and Social Power

questions.question: Oliver, you've described Mrs Woodburn's mimicry as a form of surveillance—as the only lens through which you can actually *see* the Archdeacon clearly. But here's what I keep coming back to: he's standing right there in the room, she takes him off to his face, the whole house is shaking with laughter, and he never finds out. If mimicry is power, how powerful can it really be when the target just... walks away untouched?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to commit hard to his strongest claim about wit as real social power, setting up the direct contradiction with Rosen's pacification thesis and Leigh's moral-futility argument

questions.question: Daniel, I want to read something you flagged—'She had none of the steady force, the persevering energy'—because you're saying Oliphant is being quite explicit there, that entertainment talent is almost definitionally the *opposite* of power. But doesn't that make the novel a little too comfortable? If wit is just the consolation prize for the powerless, why does it feel like Oliphant is *enjoying* every second of these scenes?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to account for the obvious pleasure in Oliphant's comic writing, which sits awkwardly with his pacification thesis, and invite Trevelyan to jump in on the enjoyment question

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read Lucilla's complete lack of humour not as a flaw but as a sign of serious moral character—you've actually used the word 'argument' for what Oliphant is doing here, not just suggestion. But here's the uncomfortable bit: Oliphant gives us Mrs Woodburn's mimicry remembered more vividly than the Archdeacon himself. If earnest action is the real virtue, why does Oliphant make the *wit* the thing that lasts?
questions.intent: Push Leigh on the tension between his conservative moral reading and Oliphant's evident delight in performance's staying power—targeting the 'remembered more clearly' passage—and create the opening for Trevelyan's counter about Lucilla's spiritual poverty

questions.question: Daniel, you flagged a comparison I find genuinely disturbing—the barrister calling executions 'a famous amusement for a country town' right alongside all this talk of wit and entertainment. Are you saying Carlingford doesn't actually distinguish between laughing at an Archdeacon and laughing at a hanging? Because that's quite a dark place to take this novel.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to land his most provocative claim about wit normalising the existing order, including its cruelties—likely to provoke strong disagreement from Trevelyan, who reads the barrister's line as savage irony rather than equivalence

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our pre-chat that I can't let go: that a world run entirely on Lucilla's principles would be *unbearably dull and morally incomplete*. Edmund is going to hate that. But I want you to make that case—what exactly is lost when you build a community that has no room for the person with the ear for human contradiction?
questions.intent: Invite Trevelyan's full provocation about Lucilla's joylessness as spiritual poverty, setting up a direct collision with Leigh's defence of seriousness as virtue and giving Rosen the chance to complicate both by asking who exactly gets to enjoy Mrs Woodburn's gifts

steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way disagreement at its core: Trevelyan thinks wit is real power and its absence in Lucilla is a loss; Rosen thinks wit is the mechanism of social pacification and therefore a tool of the system; Leigh thinks wit is morally inferior to earnest action and Oliphant knows it. Push each of them toward their most uncomfortable implications—Trevelyan on why power that leaves the Archdeacon untouched deserves the name; Rosen on why Oliphant writes these scenes with such obvious relish if she's diagnosing them as hollow; Leigh on why the mimicry outlasts the man if performance is so morally empty. The barrister-executions passage is the wildcard that can reset the whole conversation if it's getting too genteel. Use it.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's claim that 'mimicry is surveillance' directly contradicts Rosen's claim that the Archdeacon 'remains structurally unchanged, unknowing, and unmoved'—force them to argue about whether seeing through someone counts as power if nothing changes

Leigh's defence of Lucilla's humourlessness as moral seriousness collides head-on with Trevelyan's reading of it as spiritual poverty—this is the segment's sharpest fault line and should be surfaced explicitly

Rosen's pacification thesis ('laughter is the sound of the system working perfectly') ought to unsettle Trevelyan's celebration of wit as transgressive—ask Trevelyan directly whether Mrs Woodburn's indispensability to Carlingford society is evidence of power or of co-option

All three experts cite the same passage—'the house shook with restrained laughter'—and read it completely differently: Rosen sees pacification, Leigh sees futility, Trevelyan sees barely-contained subversion. That single passage could anchor a genuinely productive three-way clash if introduced at the right moment

segment_name: Moral Depth and Domestic Virtue: The Novel's Ethical Argument

questions.question: Oliver, you said before we started that the moral depth in this novel lives in the narrator's *tone*, not Lucilla's soul. That's a pretty provocative claim. Can you read us that line—'like every lofty character, could act but according to her own nature'—and tell us exactly what you're hearing in it? Because on the page it looks like a compliment.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the ironic double-reading aloud, establishing the central tension between admiration and mockery that will give Edmund and Daniel something to push against

questions.question: Edmund, you heard that—and I suspect you want to push back hard. You've been arguing that fidelity is a virtue *in itself*, regardless of whether the person you're loyal to deserves it. But doesn't that make Lucilla's goodness completely untethered from consequences? She could be loyal to genuinely terrible people and that'd still count as a lofty character?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to defend the Stoic/Burkean reading and draw out the ancient-virtue claim, while setting up Daniel's class critique

questions.question: Daniel, you flagged the word 'scorned' in that line—'she scorned to flinch or run away'—and you said it's doing something quite nasty, that it's not just about Lucilla's perseverance but a moral judgment on women who *can't* afford to stay. Can you unpack that? Because Oliver hears Austen-like comedy there, Edmund hears genuine heroism—and you're hearing something else entirely.
questions.intent: Get Daniel to deliver the class-mechanics argument through a specific word rather than abstraction, and force a three-way collision on a single phrase

questions.question: Edmund, let me put Daniel's sharpest point to you directly: he's saying Lucilla's constancy only *looks* like virtue because she has the money and position to stay put—that the novel naturalizes class privilege as moral heroism. Can you genuinely separate those two things? Is there a version of Lucilla's loyalty that would hold up if she were, say, one of the women the novel imagines fleeing to become a governess?
questions.intent: Push Edmund to either defend the virtue-independent-of-circumstance claim or concede ground to the materialist reading—a productive dilemma

questions.question: I want to end on the passage all three of you flagged—c46 paragraph 43—where Oliphant lays out the bind: Lucilla can't give up ambition and can't commit to selfless devotion either. Oliver, you said the novel doesn't pretend there's an easy answer there. Daniel says it's a rationalization dressed up as an ethical dilemma. Edmund says it's mature moral imagination. Who's right? Or is that actually the same observation wearing three different hats?
questions.intent: Force a synthesis moment that lets all three positions collide on the same passage, and potentially reveal that the disagreement is about what we want from novels rather than what Oliphant is doing

steering_notes: The productive fault line here is not really about Lucilla—it's about what counts as moral complexity in fiction. Edmund wants virtue to be real and ancient; Daniel wants the novel to answer for its ideology; Oliver wants Oliphant to be an ironist rather than a moralist. Keep pushing them to argue through specific words and phrases rather than positions, because that's where the real heat is. If the conversation gets too abstract, pull it back to a line. The word 'scorned' and the phrase 'lofty character' are your best anchors. Watch for the moment when Edmund and Daniel are actually agreeing that the novel is doing something ideological—they just disagree about whether that's a bug or a feature—and name it when it happens.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that the moral depth is in the narrator's tone rather than Lucilla's soul directly challenges Edmund's reading of Lucilla as a genuinely Stoic figure—Edmund will want to argue that irony and admiration are not mutually exclusive, which is worth prolonging
Daniel's reading of 'scorned' as contempt for women who leave is the sharpest factual disagreement with Oliver's Austen-comedy reading of the same phrase—make them argue the word, not the theory

Edmund's claim that Oliphant 'refuses to psychologize' Lucilla and Daniel's claim that the novel naturalizes her power as virtue are almost mirror images of the same observation—surface this because it could produce the best moment of unexpected agreement
The governess passage that Daniel flags as revealing material conditions is one Oliver and Edmund have not foregrounded—asking Edmund to address it directly could shift the whole conversation

questions.question: Oliver, there's this moment where Lucilla ends up — and I love the phrasing — 'in the arms of a man with a beard.' That detail of the beard keeps jumping out at me. Is Oliphant doing something serious with something that looks like a throwaway joke?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to make his case for the beard as functional grotesque — signals Tom's transformation, makes the kiss permissible — and establish his core argument that comedy and pathos are running on the same line here

questions.question: Edmund, you've zeroed in on that line — 'She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple, unlucky fellow' — and you read it as Oliphant genuinely meaning it, not winking at us. What does it mean to call the capacity for pity a form of genius?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's claim that Lucilla's genius is moral not social — her ability to feel real pity is the highest thing in the novel — which sets up a direct collision with Daniel's reading of that same passage as ideological naturalization

questions.question: Daniel, you're going to have a problem with all of this, aren't you. Because Edmund is reading Lucilla's 'Poor Tom!' as genuine compassion, Oliver is reading it as emotional complexity — and you're reading the exact same passage and seeing something much darker. What are the rest of us missing?
questions.intent: Let Daniel detonate his argument about the asymmetry of the scene — Lucilla's comfort derived from her superior position, Tom's exile reframed as romantic devotion — and force the other two to respond

questions.question: Oliver, Daniel is essentially saying that Tom's big declaration — 'There never was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if you had told me' — isn't devotion, it's a man narrating his own structural powerlessness as love. Can Oliphant's prose actually carry both of those things at once, or do you have to pick a side?
questions.intent: Force Oliver to either defend the prose as genuinely holding both readings in suspension or concede to Daniel's framing — and push Edmund to clarify whether sincerity and exploitation can coexist in the same sentence

questions.question: Edmund, here's what I keep coming back to: Lucilla cries — and the narrator tells us it's 'partly for grief, and partly because of the flutter of agitation, and something like joy.' Oliver says that word flutter is Oliphant at her best. Daniel says 'something like joy' is Lucilla keeping emotional distance while performing feeling. Who's right about those tears?
questions.intent: Triangulate the central disagreement — is the mixed-emotion passage a sign of Oliphant's psychological generosity, her theatrical genius, or the texture of upper-class emotional management — and let all three experts fight over a single short passage

steering_notes: The real engine of this segment is that all three experts are quoting the same three passages and reading them almost entirely differently. Push toward that: get them responding to each other's interpretations of specific words — 'flutter,' 'something like,' 'Poor Tom!' — rather than restating general positions. Oliver and Edmund are natural allies against Daniel, but they're also not identical: Oliver is defending the prose as performance, Edmund is defending Lucilla as morally serious. Let that internal tension surface. Daniel's read is the most provocative but risks feeling schematic — give Edmund and Oliver room to challenge him on whether ideology can account for the comedy, and whether Oliphant's irony might be more knowing than Daniel allows. Keep it concrete: words on the page, not abstractions.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's reading of 'Poor Tom!' as ideological naturalization directly contradicts Edmund's reading of the same line as evidence of genuine moral genius — these two should be asked to address each other's interpretation explicitly

Oliver's claim that the beard is 'functional grotesque' signaling real transformation sits in tension with Daniel's argument that Tom's transformation serves Lucilla's narrative rather than Tom's own reality — worth surfacing

Edmund and Oliver both want to quote Tom's declaration of devotion as sincere and touching; Daniel reads it as structural powerlessness dressed as sentiment — forcing all three to discuss one sentence together should produce the sharpest radio moment

Oliver's insistence that the narrator 'trusts us' without explaining the scene is worth testing against Daniel's argument that the narrator's trust is itself ideological — naturalizing what should be questioned

segment_name: Closing: The Limits and Legacies of Lucilla's World

questions.question: Edmund, you've described Oliphant as a moralist in the line of Johnson — someone interested in Lucilla's *soul*, not her social function. But there's this phrase in c24:p85: 'People who like to discover the alloy which blends with all human motives.' That word 'like' is doing something odd, isn't it? Is she inviting us to find the alloy, or gently mocking the people who go looking for it?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to commit to his reading of Oliphant as sincere moralist, which opens the door for Oliver to argue the narrator is winking at us, and Daniel to say the alloy IS the class mechanism

questions.question: Oliver, you said we should read that 'loftier vanity' passage aloud and hear the music of self-deception — that it *sounds* noble, *is* noble, and is also pure vanity, all at once. But isn't that a bit convenient? Are you saying the novel refuses to judge Lucilla, or that it's just very good at *appearing* to refuse?
questions.intent: Push Oliver to sharpen his irony reading and distinguish it from Edmund's moral reading — they both claim the passage is sophisticated but for opposite reasons

questions.question: Daniel, you want to read 'the natural confidence of genius in its own powers' as class position dressed up as talent. But here's what I keep getting stuck on — Lucilla *does* reorganize Carlingford. Things *do* happen. Does it matter whether that's genius or inherited authority? Is there a version of this novel where the distinction even exists?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to engage with the question of whether his structural reading erases something both Oliver and Edmund think is genuinely there — Lucilla's energy, whatever its source

questions.question: There's that line about Lucilla finding that 'many of her most able efforts turned to other people's profit.' Daniel, you said the novel almost names what's happening there — that charity is extraction. But Edmund hears that as Oliphant grieving over uncontrollable consequences, and Oliver hears it as measured, tender observation. Are all three of you looking at the same sentence?
questions.intent: Create a direct three-way collision on a single passage — get all three experts to articulate why their reading is the correct one and expose the real disagreement underneath

questions.question: Last question, and I want to put it to Edmund first: if Oliphant's deepest claim is that mixed motive is just *what human excellence looks like* — the alloy is the gold, basically — then what's the legacy of Lucilla's world? Does Carlingford end up better or worse for having had her? Does the novel even care?
questions.intent: Draw out the closing stakes of all three readings — Edmund's moral, Oliver's comic-ironic, Daniel's structural — and let the experts disagree about what Oliphant thinks the cost of Lucilla's genius actually is

steering_notes: The real disagreement in this segment isn't about Lucilla — it's about what kind of writer Oliphant is. Edmund thinks she's a moralist, Oliver thinks she's a comic ironist, Daniel thinks she's a social critic who doesn't quite know what she's uncovered. Keep pressing them to specify: which Oliphant are you reading? Try to get all three onto the same passage at the same time at least once — the 'loftier vanity' passage in c24:p85 is the flashpoint. Don't let anyone retreat into summary; push for the specific word or phrase that commits them to their reading.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund and Oliver both want to quote 'the pleasure of exercising a great faculty' but hear completely different things — Edmund hears genuine praise of Lucilla's gift, Oliver hears the music of self-deception. Get them to say why the other is wrong.

Daniel's claim that 'genius' is just class position directly contradicts Edmund's insistence that Oliphant is interested in Lucilla's soul, not social machinery. This is the sharpest disagreement in the room and needs at least one direct exchange.

Oliver's 'observational tenderness' reading of the 'turned to other people's profit' line sits somewhere between Edmund's grief and Daniel's extraction thesis — he might actually be the broker here, or he might get pulled apart by both sides.
